case_study_insert.main_stem: Copperbowl Food Hall (CFH) is a worker cooperative in the hospitality and food hall sector, employing a workforce of 52. Founded in 2016 by Rosa Delgado, CFH runs a 14-stall food hall in the dockside quarter and uses a flat organisational structure with democratic leadership. The co-op plans to invest $950,000 in a second food hall at the Old Market, financed by a $550,000 community share issue and $400,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $180,000 a year, a variable cost of $9 a unit and a selling price of $15, and currently produces 45,000 units a year. CFH faces two operational problems: food waste running at 13.6% of ingredients and rising quality complaints across its 14 stalls.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Quality/Waste Report — October 2026: Copperbowl served 41,000 meals last quarter across 14 stalls at an average transaction value of $12.60. Food waste ran at 13.6% of ingredients by value, down from 15.2% a year ago; customer complaints fell from 52 to 33 per month; the defect rate on prepared dishes is 2.1%. Footfall counters recorded 210,000 visits last quarter. A survey of 800 shoppers found 69% cite local sourcing as a priority and 62% would pay $1.00 extra for low-waste meals. On-the-job training in portion control is proposed for stallholders; off-the-job workshops at the culinary college cost $700 per stallholder.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Copperbowl Food Hall as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank raised the base interest rate from 4.6% to 5.3%, increasing borrowing costs and raising the return expected by community share investors. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.0% from $11.70 to $12.40 per hour from April 2026. (3) Fresh-produce and protein input costs have risen 11.3% year-on-year, food-price inflation stands at 7.9%, while consumer spending at food halls grew 5.2% and waste-reduction grants of up to $25,000 are available for reusable-packaging projects.

questions.question_text: CFH plans to finance part of the Old Market food hall with a $550,000 community share issue. Explain two advantages for CFH of using retained profit to fund the expansion instead of the community share issue.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Retained profit avoids creating new community shares and the dividend expectations they carry, so the $400,000 stays inside the co-op to cushion the build and tackle the 13.6% food-waste problem. Unlike a share issue, it keeps member voting power undiluted — every member retains an equal stake in how the Old Market site is run, which protects Rosa Delgado's democratic leadership model.

Point 2: Retained profit costs nothing in issue administration, member communications or return-of-capital expectations, and is available immediately — important while the base rate of 5.3% raises the hurdle for external finance and share-investor expectations. Using profit the co-op already earned demonstrates prudence to members, building support for the second food hall ahead of the member vote, keeps member returns steady, and avoids pressure on stallholders to slash portion quality or local-sourcing standards to fund new distributions or service any new obligations or member-return expectations this year.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development applied to CFH's financing decision and co-op governance.

questions.question_text: CFH is launching the Old Market food hall. Consider a citywide print and radio campaign, opening-week stall discounts, or social media influencer marketing. Which should CFH choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Citywide print and radio: Broad reach across the dockside and Old Market catchments builds launch awareness quickly and suits a co-op wanting all residents to feel welcome at the new site. However, costs are high relative to a $950,000 build, audiences are untargeted (not every listener eats out), response is hard to measure, and the message cannot showcase the 14 stalls' stories or the 69% local-sourcing appeal the way video can.

Opening-week stall discounts: Deep opening discounts drive trial and footfall fast — food halls thrive on crowd energy, and 210,000 visits last quarter prove demand is already strong. But discounting cuts the $15 price and the $6 contribution per unit precisely when CFH must fund the build, attracts bargain-hunters rather than loyal regulars, and can train customers to wait for promotions instead of paying the $1.00 low-waste premium that 62% of shoppers support.

Social media influencer marketing: Food creators can film stall walkthroughs, local-sourcing stories and the $1.00 low-waste option, reaching the 69% who prioritise local produce and the 62% willing to pay a premium. Engagement is measurable (footfall, sales per stall, premium uptake), costs are low, and the content reinforces the co-op's community narrative better than any advertisement.

Recommendation: CFH should choose social media influencer marketing. It targets the exact ethical-food segment CFH's own research identified, preserves the margin needed to fund the Old Market build, and builds durable community loyalty. Print and radio are rejected as untargeted and hard to measure for a $950,000 cooperative launch; opening-week discounts are rejected as a margin-eroding tactic best limited to a single tasting weekend, not the core launch strategy.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge or outline of the promotional options with minimal context.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of CFH with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of CFH with a well-justified recommendation explaining why print and radio and opening discounts are rejected.

questions.question_text: CFH's quality complaints across its 14 stalls remain too high. Explain two benefits for CFH of using democratic leadership to improve quality consistency among stallholders.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Democratic leadership gives all 14 stallholders a voice in food-safety standards, portion sizes and recipe specifications, meeting esteem needs (Maslow) and raising commitment to common standards. Co-op members who help set the rules police each other informally, directly attacking the 2.1% defect rate and the complaint rate, without an expensive external inspection regime.

Point 2: Involving stallholders surfaces practical waste and quality fixes — standardised pre-prep volumes that cut the 13.6% food waste — and strengthens Herzberg's motivators (achievement, recognition, responsibility). Members trained this way become quality ambassadors for the Old Market launch; the flat democratic structure keeps decisions fast, lifts accountability across all 14 stalls, and gives CFH's workforce of 52 a consistent playbook to scale into the second site without an expensive quality-assurance manager, and turns every stallholder into a shareholder-owner with a genuine stake in every dish that leaves the pass, every complaint resolved and every gram of waste measured and weighed honestly.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to CFH's defect rate, waste and co-op structure.

questions.question_text: CFH must cut food waste through staff training. Consider on-the-job training in portion control or off-the-job workshops at the culinary college. Which should CFH choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Portion-control coaching at each stall during live service is specific to CFH's own menus, free of course fees, keeps the 14 stalls trading at full speed through the lunch rush, and can be led by the strongest stallholders as internal mentors — reinforcing the co-op's democratic knowledge-sharing culture. Drawbacks: coaching quality varies between stalls, bad habits may spread, and no formal certificate is recorded for board audits or the Old Market licensing file.

Off-the-job workshops: The culinary college workshops at $700 per stallholder provide structured, expert-led portioning and waste-prevention curricula with recognised certification; the survey evidence — 69% prioritising local sourcing and 62% backing the $1.00 low-waste premium — shows a market for certified low-waste practice. It costs money (14 stallholders × $700 = $9,800) and requires staggered rotas, but upskills everyone to one auditable standard.

Decision: CFH should choose off-the-job workshops as the core training, reinforced by on-the-job coaching at each stall. Waste of 13.6% of ingredient value is CFH's single biggest margin leak, and certified, uniformly applied skills are worth $9,800 against thousands in wasted produce circulating every week — cost recovery in well under two months if waste falls just one percentage point. On-the-job training alone is rejected as the primary route because variable coaching quality cannot deliver the certified consistency the Old Market launch and waste-reduction grants of up to $25,000 may require; coaching should follow the workshops, not replace them as the source of the standard, the audit certificate or the grant evidence.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to CFH.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of one or both training methods in the context of CFH.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both training methods in the context of CFH with a well-justified decision covering cost, waste and audit requirements.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how CFH's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $180,000 ÷ ($15 − $9) = $180,000 ÷ $6 = 30,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 30,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $15 − $9 = $6.00. Answer: contribution per unit is $6.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways CFH's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. CFH's management can compare the 30,000-unit break-even output with actual output of 45,000 units to confirm a comfortable margin of safety of 15,000 units before committing to the second food hall at the Old Market.
2. Contribution per unit of $6 lets CFH model the removal of low-selling menu lines, and shows how the $1.00 low-waste premium lifts contribution to $7 on qualifying dishes for the 62% of shoppers who back it.
3. Fixed-cost knowledge of $180,000 helps the co-op test whether a $550,000 community share issue is realistic given share-investor return expectations and the Old Market build's early overheads.
4. Unit cost data ($180,000 ÷ 45,000 units + $9 = $13.00 a unit) lets CFH benchmark stall-level margins, find the worst waste offenders (13.6% of ingredients) and target them with portion-control support first.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 30,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $6 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: margin of safety (15,000 units vs 45,000 output) confirms expansion headroom; contribution modelling supports the $1.00 low-waste premium and menu engineering; fixed-cost cover of $180,000 tests the $550,000 share issue; and the $13.00 unit cost benchmarks stall efficiency and waste control across the 14 stalls serving 210,000 quarterly visits.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method, 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate CFH's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has CFH's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.64 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.70 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 1.04 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.12 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $85,000 inventories + $40,000 trade receivables + $105,000 cash = $230,000; 2025 current assets = $95,000 + $55,000 + $130,000 = $280,000. 2024 = $230,000 ÷ $140,000 = 1.64 : 1; 2025 = $280,000 ÷ $165,000 = 1.70 : 1. Excluding inventories: 2024 = ($230,000 − $85,000) ÷ $140,000 = $145,000 ÷ $140,000 = 1.04 : 1; 2025 = ($280,000 − $95,000) ÷ $165,000 = $185,000 ÷ $165,000 = 1.12 : 1.

Evaluation: Liquidity improved steadily. Cash strengthened from $105,000 to $130,000 on strong trading (41,000 meals last quarter) and receivables rose only modestly ($40,000 to $55,000, mainly stallholders settling weekly). Inventories crept up $10,000, reflecting deliberate local-produce stocks; current liabilities rose 18% to $165,000 as supplier credit expanded ahead of the Old Market fit-out. The inventory-excluded measure improved from 1.04 to 1.12 — confirming the co-op can meet short-term debts without selling perishable stock, vital for a business whose 13.6% waste risk makes inventory relatively fast-perishing. Non-current assets nearly doubled to $2,150,000 consistent with the build, and capital employed reached $2,265,000.

Conclusion: CFH's financial position has improved on both measures; the improvement is clean, does not depend on perishable inventory, and supports proceeding with the Old Market launch — provided CFH tightens weekly settlement with stallholders and stops 13.6% ingredient waste from eroding the stronger cash position.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the current ratio and acid test ratio for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years combined with detailed evaluation of inventory, receivables and liabilities movements and a justified conclusion on whether CFH's financial position improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for CFH of introducing reusable-packaging across all 14 stalls.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Reusable-packaging matches the 62% of shoppers willing to pay $1.00 extra for low-waste meals and the 69% who prioritise local sourcing, letting CFH capture a sustainability premium on top of the $12.60 average transaction value and apply for the waste-reduction grant of up to $25,000 — reinforcing the co-op's community brand ahead of the Old Market launch, deepening member pride and local press coverage.

Disadvantage: Deposit handling, washing logistics and breakages raise handling costs and hygiene-breach risk; if deposits deter price-sensitive shoppers or stallholders resist the extra admin, CFH sells fewer units and contribution ($6 per unit) falls. The 2.1% defect rate and 13.6% food waste already strain operations, so bolting on a packaging-return loop without new staff (workforce of 52) could overwhelm stall teams, reduce Friday-lunch trade and damage the customer experience that drives 210,000 quarterly visits and the premium the 62% already accept.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to CFH's waste data, research and co-op capacity.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 5.3%, the 6.0% minimum wage increase and the 11.3% rise in fresh-produce costs will affect CFH. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.6% to 5.3%): CFH's $550,000 community share issue carries no bank interest, though investor return expectations rise; any start-up loan for the Old Market fit-out arranged at 5.3% costs more, and cautious consumers may trade down to cheaper lunch deals. The net effect is modest and partially blunts through the $25,000 waste-reduction grant opportunity.

Minimum wage increase (6.0%, to $12.40): Front-of-house, cleaning and junior kitchen roles across 14 stalls sit near the minimum. If, for illustration, 30 of the 52 staff are near it, the extra $0.70 per hour costs roughly $42,000 a year — a meaningful recurring bite out of the $6 contribution per unit, though one a democratic co-op can attack through better portion control, lifting labour productivity rather than simply paying more for the same hours.

Fresh-produce and protein costs (+11.3%): Ingredients dominate the $9 unit cost. If, for illustration, half the unit cost is produce ($4.50), an 11.3% rise adds about $0.51 per unit — roughly $23,000 a year at 45,000 units — compounding with 7.9% food-price inflation and arriving every single day, on every meal, unlike wages and unlike interest.

Conclusion: The 11.3% rise in fresh-produce and protein costs will have the greatest impact. It recurs across all 45,000 units, erodes the $6 contribution immediately, and stacks with 7.9% food inflation that CFH can only partly claw back through the $1.00 low-waste premium and menu re-engineering. The wage rise is second — significant but offsettable through productivity gains and democratic scheduling — while interest is smallest and manageable via the grant and the community share structure. CFH should lock supply contracts, engineer portion sizes, and re-price the premium range before April 2026.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to CFH.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on CFH's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of CFH with a well-justified judgement that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.
